title: Choosing friends
hookLine: a person is on the religion of his close friend (Abu Dawud)
tomorrow: why would an angel stop a man on his way to see a friend?

cards: A new group chat full of strangers, all headed to the same campus in the fall. Within an hour, smaller chats split off. Where you land matters more than it looks.
The Prophet ﷺ told it as a scene at a market. You're walking between two stalls. On one side, a perfume seller.
On the other, a blacksmith pumping his bellows. You haven't bought anything. You're just standing there.
And already something is happening to you.

teach.h: PERFUME, EVEN IF YOU DON'T BUY.
teach.b: Here's the scene as Sahih al-Bukhari keeps it. The perfume seller might give you some for free. Or you might buy some.
And even if you do neither, you walk away smelling good. The blacksmith's bellows might burn your clothes.

teach.h: SMOKE, EVEN IF YOU DON'T BURN.
teach.b: And even if they don't, you walk away smelling of smoke. That, the Prophet says, is a good companion and a bad one. Nobody has to say a word.

A hadith in Sunan Abu Dawud says it outright: a person is on the way of their close friend, so look carefully at whom you take as a close friend. The word is khalil, the close friend, not everyone in the group chat.
You can be kind to a whole class and still choose your inner few with care. And the perfume isn't a label.
It's what rubs off: patience, honesty, a friend who reminds you it's time to pray, or tells you the truth when it stings.
The blacksmith isn't a villain, either; he's working. The question is only what you carry home on your clothes.
One to tell a friend tonight: in the Prophet's picture, you don't have to buy anything to come home smelling of it.

how: Muslims quote the perfume seller and the blacksmith when talking about friends, and speak of good company, suhba, as something that shapes faith over time.

o: picking your close friends by what rubs off
keeping as many friends as you possibly can
making friends only with people like you

games.q: what goes with what — tap the pairs.
p: you smell good, even without buying

s: the hadith means you should only befriend people just like you
it's about what rubs off from the close friend you choose: perfume or smoke.
in the parable, you can come home smelling of perfume without buying any
the Abu Dawud hadith is about your close friend, not everyone you meet

games.q: a new teammate is hilarious but mocks anyone who studies. a quieter one always helps you prep. who do you sit with on the long bus ride?
o: the funny one; friends are mostly for a good time.
neither; keep to yourself so nothing rubs off.
the one who helps you prep, and stay friendly with both.
games.why: the parable isn't about shutting people out; it's about where you stand longest. kind to everyone, close to the perfume.

practice: If there's anything with a scent near you, soap, coffee, a sleeve that still smells of someone's house, hold it close and breathe it in. Notice how it stays a little after you set it down.
Then bring to mind one friend whose goodness has rubbed off on you, and name to yourself exactly what they left on you.

wordCard.voice: Choosing friends: picking your close few with care, because what they carry gets on you. Perfume, or smoke.

orig.note: Arabic: a close friend, an intimate; the word in the Abu Dawud hadith.

carryVoice: Your line: choose friends well, because by evening it's in your clothes. That's five of ten.

sources.ref: Sahih al-Bukhari 2101 (also 5534; the perfume seller and the blacksmith's bellows)
Sunan Abu Dawud 4833 (a person is on the religion of their close friend, so look at whom you befriend)
